summary: Kosovo waives visas for EU and Schengen-area citizens, a broad Western list and its Balkan neighbours for up to 90 days, and admits holders of valid multi-entry Schengen, US or UK visas for short visits without a Kosovo visa; remaining nationalities apply at a Kosovo embassy.

passportValidity.text: Your passport should be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from Kosovo — carrying 6 months’ validity is safest; ID-card entry is available to EU and Western Balkans citizens.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Diaspora of the Republic of Kosovo

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not checked for visa-free visitors, but visa applicants must show travel health insurance for the stay — and normal travel insurance is strongly advised as public healthcare facilities are limited.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Diaspora of the Republic of Kosovo

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Diaspora of the Republic of Kosovo

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared to Kosovo Customs on entry and exit.

notes: Standard duty-free allowances apply for tobacco and alcohol — roughly 200 cigarettes and 1 litre of spirits per adult; confirm current limits with Kosovo Customs.
Vehicles need valid insurance recognised in Kosovo — many European Green Cards exclude Kosovo, and border insurance must then be bought on arrival.

payments.text: Kosovo uses the euro even though it is not in the eurozone. Cards work in Pristina and Prizren hotels, supermarkets and bigger restaurants, but much of daily life runs on cash — carry euros in small denominations, especially outside the cities.

safety.text: Kosovo is generally safe for visitors, with low street crime and a famously welcoming attitude to travellers. Tensions occasionally flare in the Serb-majority northern municipalities around Mitrovica — follow local advice and avoid protests.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Kosovo Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September is warm and lively, ideal for Pristina’s café scene, Prizren’s old town and hiking in the Rugova and Sharr mountains; winters are cold but bring cheap skiing at Brezovica.

tips.text: Serbia treats direct arrival into Kosovo as an illegal entry into its territory: if you plan to continue from Kosovo into Serbia, enter Serbia first (or route via a third country) — travellers with only a Kosovo entry stamp are routinely refused at Serbian crossings.
The Serb-majority northern municipalities around Mitrovica see periodic unrest — check current advice before visiting the north and stay away from demonstrations and roadblocks.
If you hold a valid multi-entry Schengen visa (already used once) or a valid US or UK visa or residence permit, you can enter Kosovo without a Kosovo visa for a short visit of up to 15 days.
Driving in? Check whether your Green Card insurance actually covers Kosovo — many policies exclude it, and you must then buy local border insurance on arrival; keep the receipt for checkpoints.
Kosovo runs on euro cash outside the big cities — keep small notes handy for taxis, bakeries and mountain guesthouses, and expect some places to struggle to change €50 notes.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Kosovo?
faq.answer: Probably not: Kosovo waives visas for up to 90 days for EU and Schengen-area citizens, the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and many others, plus its Western Balkans neighbours. Holders of valid multi-entry Schengen, US or UK visas can also enter visa-free for up to 15 days. Other nationalities apply at a Kosovo embassy.

faq.question: Can I enter Kosovo with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Yes — holders of a valid multi-entry Schengen visa that has already been used in the Schengen Area (or a Schengen residence permit) can enter Kosovo without a Kosovo visa for up to 15 days. The same applies to valid US and UK visas and residence permits.

faq.question: Can I travel between Kosovo and Serbia?
faq.answer: Crossings operate, but direction matters: Serbia does not recognise Kosovo’s international border points, so if you entered Kosovo directly (by air or from Albania, North Macedonia or Montenegro), Serbia may refuse you entry as having entered Serbia illegally. Visit Serbia first, or route through a third country.

faq.question: What currency is used in Kosovo?
faq.answer: The euro is Kosovo’s official currency, even though Kosovo is not an EU or eurozone member. Cards are fine in city hotels and supermarkets, but carry euro cash in small denominations for everything else; in a few Serb-majority areas the Serbian dinar also circulates unofficially.

faq.question: Is Kosovo part of the Schengen Area or the EU?
faq.answer: No — Kosovo is outside the EU and Schengen, so days spent there do not count against your Schengen 90/180-day allowance. That makes Kosovo (like its Balkan neighbours) a popular stop for travellers resetting their Schengen clock.

faq.question: How are Kosovar passport holders treated abroad?
faq.answer: Kosovo citizens travel visa-free to the EU and Schengen Area for 90 days in any 180 with a biometric passport (since January 2024), but several countries that do not recognise Kosovo still refuse or restrict the passport — check each destination individually.
